name: Freight Trains
description: Rail freight in Iran encompasses domestic goods movements and international import, export, and transit traffic. Understanding its performance requires distinguishing the weight carried from transport work measured in tonne-kilometres.

seo.title: Freight Trains in Iran: Traffic, Measurement and Border Coordination
seo.description: Understand Iranian rail freight statistics and the coordination required to move goods across international railway borders.

content.heading: What rail freight statistics measure
content.content:
Iran's railway freight performance can be described using different measures. Tonnes describe the weight transported; tonne-kilometres combine weight with the distance it travels. These measures answer different questions and should not be substituted for one another. The inspected statistical table reports Iran's annual railway goods transport in million tonne-kilometres and attributes the figures to the World Bank's World Development Indicators. Its latest displayed observation is 2021, leaving a substantial gap between the available series and this page's research cutoff. [s1]

The observations below describe transport work, rather than the number of trains, containers, or shipments. They also do not isolate international transit from other freight. Consequently, they cannot establish the performance of an individual border crossing or trade corridor. [s1]

content.title: Iran: reported railway goods transport, 2012–2021
content.interpretation: Reported transport work increased from 22604 million tonne-kilometres in 2012 to 35963 million in 2020, before falling to 32920 million in 2021. The series does not establish subsequent performance.

content.heading: International freight requires operational agreements
content.content:
Iran participated in the Organisation for Co-operation between Railways' international freight coordination meeting in February–March 2024. The organisation, commonly abbreviated OSJD, reported that participating railways agreed traffic volumes by border crossing, commodity, and quarter. Additional contracts still required operational agreement that took border handling capacity into account. Agreed volumes were therefore planning commitments, not evidence that the goods had already moved. [s2]

The meeting identified practical work needed to reduce border delays: timely train formation, faster wagon and locomotive turnover, better information exchange, and correct transport documents. It also addressed returning empty wagons and avoiding the separation of container trains. These were collective priorities for participating railways; the document does not quantify each problem specifically within Iran. [s2]

For readers assessing a proposed international service, the useful questions extend beyond whether tracks connect two places. They include whether receiving railways have accepted the traffic and whether border capacity and documents are ready. The meeting record demonstrates why physical infrastructure and operational coordination must be considered together. [s2]

name: Tehran Metro
description: Tehran Metro combines urban rapid-transit routes with suburban rail connections. Its development began with the western suburban service in 1999, followed by central urban metro operations in 2000.

seo.title: Tehran Metro: Urban Lines and Suburban Connections
seo.description: An introduction to Tehran Metro's development, interchange structure, suburban services, and airport branches.

content.heading: A network built in stages
content.content:
Tehran's rail system developed through both suburban and urban services. The western suburban route, known as Line 5, opened between Tehran and Karaj in March 1999. The first central section of Line 2 followed in February 2000, connecting Sadeghieh with Imam Khomeini. Line 1 began carrying passengers in 2001. These separate openings explain why accounts of the system's beginning may distinguish suburban rail from the urban metro. [s1]

Expansion was gradual rather than a single opening of complete lines. The specialist chronology records extensions and individual station openings separately. This distinction matters: an inaugurated route section does not establish that every intermediate station was available from its first day. [s1]

content.heading: Urban routes and regional journeys
content.content:
The system includes different kinds of railway. Line 5 provides a surface commuter connection westward, while central urban lines form an interchange network. Line 1 and Line 2 meet at Imam Khomeini. Airport access also involves distinct branches: the Mehrabad connection branches from Line 4, whereas the Imam Khomeini International Airport connection is associated with Line 1. The latter was extended to Parand in 2023. [s1]

A September 2023 industry report describes further connections across the urban network. Line 3 offers interchange with Lines 1, 4, and 6, while Line 6 links several other routes. The same report records passenger-service openings on extensions of Lines 4, 6, and 7 during 2023. Such additions matter because an extension can create a new transfer opportunity as well as bring rail service to another district. [s2]

content.heading: Infrastructure and the limits of network totals
content.content:
The September 2023 report describes standard-gauge track and a technical distinction between third-rail power on Lines 1–4 and overhead supply on Line 5. These differences reinforce that the network's common passenger identity encompasses more than one operating format. [s2]

The report also contains inconsistent classifications and apparent editing errors, including a reference to an Isfahan fare card in its Tehran entry. Its aggregate network and ridership figures are therefore not reproduced here. A current operator inventory is needed before publishing a definitive total of operational stations or route length. [s2]

For understanding Tehran, the most useful starting point is the relationship between central interchange routes and outward suburban connections. For an actual journey, however, this historical account cannot establish current branch frequencies, station availability, or operating hours. Those details require a dated service notice rather than inference from a network map.

name: Mashhad Metro
description: Mashhad's urban railway combines a segregated light-rail first line with later metro development. Airport access, interchange between lines, and a more direct connection to the Imam Reza shrine district are important elements of its documented expansion.

seo.title: Mashhad Metro: Light Rail, Interchanges and Expansion
seo.description: Explore the development of Mashhad's urban railway, from its first light-rail route to airport access and the initial Line 3 service.

content.heading: One system, different railway formats
content.content:
Mashhad's urban railway illustrates why the word metro does not always describe identical infrastructure. UrbanRail.Net identifies Line 1 as fully segregated light rail using low-floor vehicles, with both underground and surface sections. It distinguishes Line 2 as a conventional metro with high-level platforms. Segregation means the first line has its own railway alignment; surface running alone does not make it a street tram. [s1]

The specialist chronology places the first line's trial service in 2011 and its airport extension in February 2016. Line 2's initial northeastern section opened in February 2017. Its southwestward extension reached Shariati in May 2018, creating interchange with Line 1. That connection changed the relationship between the routes: passengers could transfer between them instead of using two disconnected services. [s1]

content.heading: Line 3: opening a section and improving its service
content.content:
UrbanRail.Net records the start of Line 3 trial service in May 2025, serving Shohada, Bab Ol-Javad, and the Imam Reza coach terminal. These destinations explain the initial section's role: it links a coach terminal with the central shrine area and the existing railway network. [s1]

A November 2025 Tasnim report provides a later operational milestone. Quoting municipal officials, it describes the opening of the second platform and operation with two trains, following an initial limited service. Officials reported shorter intervals and longer operating hours. These are attributed reports of service improvements at that date, rather than independently measured performance or a timetable guaranteed for subsequent years. [s2]

The Imam Reza shrine is a major Shia Muslim pilgrimage destination. In the report, municipal officials framed Line 3 as a way to improve access for both pilgrims and residents. Their claims that rail expansion would reduce congestion and improve environmental conditions express the project's intended benefits; the article does not supply an evaluation establishing those outcomes. [s2]

content.heading: Distinguishing completed links from promises
content.content:
The same November 2025 report treated Basij, the proposed interchange between Lines 1 and 3, as a future opening. UrbanRail.Net also listed its opening as scheduled rather than completed. Neither statement establishes that the transfer was available by this page's cutoff. [s1][s2]

The municipal account also discussed obtaining additional Line 1 vehicles and extending Line 3. Procurement steps and expected capacity increases should be kept separate from delivered vehicles and demonstrated passenger capacity. This distinction is particularly useful in Mashhad, where the inspected evidence shows that opening an initial section and strengthening its service were separate stages. [s2]
